answer.exemplar: The middle field is everything between the finite verb in the second field and the non-finite part of the verb at the end, and it holds the subject, the objects and any further phrases. It is unbounded in principle, so a sentence can grow there without ever becoming ungrammatical: Ich habe gestern den sehr langen Bericht an meine Kollegin in der Bibliothek nicht gelesen. The result is grammatical and unreadable, because the reader is asked to hold the whole group in mind before reaching the participle that resolves it. The first repair is to move a heavy phrase out past the participle, so Ich habe den sehr langen Bericht nicht gelesen, den meine Kollegin gestern aus der Bibliothek gebracht hat. The second is to split the sentence in two, so that each one carries a verb of its own.

questions.explanation: The middle field is the stretch of the clause between the finite verb in the second field and the non-finite part of the verb, and it holds the subject, the objects and any phrases attached to them. Nothing in the grammar limits how much can go in there, so a sentence may grow to any length and stay perfectly correct: Ich habe gestern den sehr langen Bericht an meine Kollegin in der Bibliothek nicht gelesen. What fails is the reader, who has to hold all of it before reaching the participle that resolves it. Two repairs are available. One is to move a heavy phrase out past the participle into the end field. The other is to split the sentence in two, giving each half a verb of its own, which is what a writer should prefer when the group is long enough to need it.

questions.stem: A learner has noticed that a German clause can be opened either by a conjunction that carries a subject itself or by one that leaves the subject to the main clause, and the two behave differently. Explain the difference between als and wie in that use, with one sentence of each kind, and say which one can be reversed.

answer.exemplar: The two connectives differ in whether they bring a subject with them. als introduces a clause that names the subject itself, so Ich bin größer als du compares two people and cannot be turned round, because du bin größer als ich says the other way. wie introduces a clause whose subject has to be supplied, so Ich fahre so schnell wie du can be reversed to Du fahrst so schnell wie ich, and the same is true of Ich bin so alt wie du, which becomes Du bist so alt wie ich. A learner who swaps the two produces a comparison between two people where the German only allows one, which is why the pair is worth learning as a pair.

questions.explanation: The two connectives differ in whether they bring a subject with them. als introduces a clause that names its own subject, so Ich bin größer als du compares the speaker with another person and cannot be reversed, since du bin größer als ich says the opposite. wie introduces a clause that has to be supplied with one, so Ich fahre so schnell wie du can be reversed to Du fahrst so schnell wie ich, and Ich bin so alt wie du reverses to Du bist so alt wie ich. The practical difference is that a comparison of two people with wie is symmetrical and one with als is not, and that is worth checking before a sentence is handed in.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause names its own subject, and then try the sentence with the two subjects exchanged.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The order of the three time words in a letter
questions.learningObjective: arrange the place, the date and the addressee in the order a German letter uses
questions.stem: A short business letter has to carry the place, the date and the addressee, and German has a fixed order for the three blocks at the top. Put these three blocks in the order a German letter actually uses.

options.text: Der Ort, dann das Datum, dann die Anrede des Empfängers.
Die Anrede des Empfängers, dann der Ort, dann das Datum.
Das Datum, dann der Ort, dann die Anrede des Empfängers.

questions.explanation: A German business letter follows one order at the top: the sender's place and the date, then the line with the addressee's name, and only then the text itself. The date stands above the addressee and never below it, which is the detail a writer coming from English most often gets wrong, because the English letter puts the date at the end of the block. Inside the date the order is day, month, year, and the month is written in figures while an older formal letter spelled it out.
questions.hint: Ask which block stands furthest down, and where the addressee's name belongs in relation to it.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: How the two adjectives of a comparison are both kept
questions.learningObjective: build a comparative phrase and supply the set it selects from
questions.stem: A writer needs to say that one of two trains is the faster one, and the phrase has to name the set of two before it picks from it. First say what the phrase has to do before the comparative can go in, and then write the phrase in full.

answer.exemplar: The comparative of a noun phrase cannot stand on its own in German, because a comparative says more or less than something and the something has to be named. The set comes first, as in der schnellere, and it has to be a genitive, so von den beiden Zügen becomes der schnellere von den beiden Zügen. Writing der schnellere Zug is not possible, and so is der schnellere der zwei Züge, because the set needs the genitive. The second half then supplies what it is faster than, as in der schnellere von den beiden Zügen fährt um zwei Stunden früher.

questions.explanation: A comparative in German cannot stand on its own, because a comparative means more or less than something, and the something has to be named. The set of two comes first and is put in the genitive: von den beiden Zügen, so the whole phrase is der schnellere von den beiden Zügen. Writing der schnellere Zug is not possible, because a comparative cannot take a noun directly, and der schnellere der zwei Züge fails for the same reason. The comparison then still needs its second half, which the reader supplies, as in fährt um zwei Stunden früher.
questions.hint: Ask what a comparative means that has to be named before the noun can go next to it.

questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: Reading a case ending back from a sentence
questions.learningObjective: read a case off the article and check a preposition against it
questions.stem: A sentence has to be checked, and the only clue to what a preposition requires is the ending on the noun that follows it. Which of the four phrases has an ending that agrees with a preposition which never takes the dative?

options.text: mit dem kleinen Bruder
options.misconception: carries the article of a preposition that governs the dative rather than the accusative

options.text: bei dem Arzt
options.misconception: shows the dative singular article of a masculine noun, which no other case of that noun uses

options.text: von dem Fenster
options.misconception: also shows the masculine dative article, which points the other way from the claim being tested

options.text: ohne jede Hilfe

questions.explanation: ohne takes the accusative, and in ohne jede Hilfe the indefinite article jede is accusative feminine singular, so the noun loses its ending entirely. The other three phrases all contain a dative: mit dem, bei dem and von dem, each of which is followed by a masculine noun in the dative singular. Reading the article back is therefore a reliable check, because a masculine noun in the dative is always dem and in the accusative always den, whatever preposition stands in front of it.
questions.hint: Ask which article the preposition could possibly have produced, and whether a masculine noun can take it.
